Question eight. What is k-means clustering? Place k centers, assign each point to the nearest one, move each center to the mean of its points, and repeat until nothing moves. These three centers all start in one group. After one move, two of them jump toward the other groups, and on the third pass, it settles. It minimizes the within-cluster sum of squares, which always falls as k grows, so look for the elbow. Here it drops from twenty thousand at one cluster to five sixty-seven at three, then barely moves. The silhouette score, how much nearer each point sits to its own cluster than to the next, peaks at three as well. And run several starts, or k-means plus plus, because a bad start can settle in the wrong place. More features bring trouble of their own.

Question nine. What is P C A? Principal component analysis finds the directions in which the data varies most, each at right angles to the last, and projects the data onto the first few. On the four iris measurements, scaled first, one component holds seventy-three percent of the variance, and two hold ninety-six. Four columns become two, and the species still separate. It needs centered data, and it only finds straight-line structure. Question ten. What is the curse of dimensionality? As dimensions grow, space empties out. Scatter a thousand random points. In two dimensions, a point's nearest neighbor is about sixty times closer than its farthest. In a thousand dimensions, the nearest is almost as far as the farthest. Distances stop telling points apart, and K N N and k-means suffer first. The fixes: fewer dimensions, through P C A or feature selection, and regularization. The last deep dive: which features mattered.
